articles.title: Jaws director Steven Spielberg protected 7.46 East Hampton acres with conservation easements in 2011; all 3 marsh and forest parcels are closed to development
articles.summary: US News: Steven Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in East Hampton Village in 2011, which permanently protected 7.46 acres from develo.
articles.body: Steven Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in East Hampton Village in 2011, which permanently protected 7.46 acres from development. The land sits around Georgica Cove and contains brackish tidal marsh, maritime forest, old field and shrubland.The parcels were held through a Spielberg family subsidiary called the S.A.M. Trust. The Peconic Land Trust received the conservation easements, while the Village of East Hampton approved the transaction. The three properties measure 2.45, 2.65 and 2.36 acres respectively, according to the Peconic Land Trust's 2011 newsletter.Three separate pieces of landThe properties are located around Chauncey Close and Cove Hollow Farm Road near Georgica Cove. Two of the parcels are next to one another, while the third lies across a small road. The conservation easements placed permanent restrictions on what could be done with the land, and the Peconic Land Trust said the easements prohibited vegetative screening and landscaping except when such work was needed to manage or improve natural habitat or prevent a public hazard.The land trust described the properties as remnants of the former Cove Hollow Farm, whose habitats included brackish tidal marsh and successional maritime forest, along with old fields and shrubland. The organization said the protected areas contributed to the health of Georgica Cove and Georgica Pond and provided habitat for mammals, birds, turtles and other wetland species.Spielberg lived across the waterSpielberg's family home, Quelle Farm, was on Apaquogue Road across the water from the three parcels. A December 2011 report in The East Hampton Star said Spielberg had donated the conservation easements through the S.A.M. Trust to the Peconic Land Trust. It reported that the three parcels were located in the Cove Hollow Farm neighborhood at the intersection of Chauncey Close and Ruxton Road.The East Hampton Village Board had approved the transaction at a meeting that month, with village administrator Larry Cantwell saying that the approval recognized that the easement and gift were consistent with village policies for preserving natural resources. Spielberg did not simply hand the parcels over to a public agency; instead, the conservation easements placed legally binding restrictions on development while the land remained under private ownership.The restrictions went beyond constructionThe 7.46 acres were protected from development but the restrictions extended further, as seen by the Peconic Land Trust's account, which says that landscaping was also prohibited except where it served a conservation purpose or addressed a public hazard. The parcels were valuable waterfront land, which is why that matters. The easements preserved the existing ecological communities rather than allowing the properties to be cleared or landscaped as conventional residential lots.The land trust specifically linked the protection to Georgica Cove and Georgica Pond, and its 2011 publication said the easements would help protect habitat used by numerous mammals, birds, turtles and other wetland species. The village's involvement also gave the arrangement a local planning dimension. The transaction was approved not as a public acquisition of a park, but as a conservation measure consistent with East Hampton's policies on natural resources.What did the easement change?The Peconic Land Trust's records identify the three conservation easements as covering 7.46 acres of natural habitat, and the restrictions were mainly designed to remain with the properties rather than expire when ownership changed. The three parcels needed to be preserved as they kept a section of tidal marsh, forest, old field and shrubland from being converted into a more developed residential landscape.Spielberg's role was tied to the land through the S.A.M. Trust rather than through a public park created in his name, and the conservation easements instead provided a legal mechanism to keep the three parcels undeveloped while maintaining their existing habitat. The Peconic Land Trust continues to describe conservation easements as a way of permanently protecting natural lands while ownership can remain private.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, the US removed 69 dams, reconnecting 624 miles of rivers and restoring habitat for salmon, steelhead and native fish species
articles.summary: US News: Across the United States, some rivers are beginning to flow through places where dams once stood. In 2020, 69 dams were removed across 23 states, reop.
articles.body: Across the United States, some rivers are beginning to flow through places where dams once stood. In 2020, 69 dams were removed across 23 states, reopening hundreds of miles of waterways that had been blocked for decades. Some structures had outlived the purpose for which they were built, while others had become expensive to maintain or posed growing safety concerns. For fish and wildlife, the changes could be significant, restoring access to stretches of river that had long been cut off. The work continued even as the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted construction and restoration projects across the country.According to American Rivers, from an obsolete industrial dam in Indiana to barriers affecting salmon habitat in Washington, the removals showed how decisions about ageing infrastructure can also reshape rivers, habitats and nearby communities. By the end of the year, the total number of dam removals in the US since 1912 had reached 1,797.US dam removals in 2020 addressed safety, ageing infrastructure and river restorationThe 69 removals recorded in 2020 brought the number of dams taken out across the US since 1912 to 1,797. Ohio recorded the highest number that year, with 11 removals, while Massachusetts and New York each recorded six, as reported.The work did not stop when normal construction schedules were disrupted by Covid-19. Engineers, contractors, local authorities, conservation groups and other partners continued with projects where it was possible to do so safely.There was no single reason for taking a dam out. In some places, a structure had become obsolete. Elsewhere, the issue was public safety, fish passage or the cost of maintaining ageing infrastructure. A few projects combined several of these concerns.Why removal of obsolete dams became US priorityMore than 90,000 dams are estimated to stand across rivers in the US. They range from major pieces of infrastructure to relatively small barriers that were built for mills, water supplies, recreation or other local purposes.As these structures age, their original uses can disappear while the costs and risks associated with keeping them remain. Some also interfere with the movement of fish and alter the flow and ecological character of rivers.According to American Rivers, the failure of Michigan's Edenville Dam in May 2020 brought the safety issue into sharp focus. The collapse led to extensive flooding and became another reminder of the risks associated with ageing infrastructure. Reportedly, a United Nations report published around the same period also warned about the growing problems posed by ageing dams and water infrastructure.In many cases, the work is also tied to local economic activity. A study from the University of North Carolina estimated that ecological restoration directly employed about 126,000 people nationally and supported another 100,000 jobs indirectly, with the sector contributing around $25 billion to the US economy each year.How a 2020 dam removal restored 16 miles of salmon habitatOne of the larger examples from 2020 took place on the Middle Fork Nooksack River near Bellingham, Washington.There, an old water diversion dam was removed and a new water intake installed. The change opened roughly 16 miles of previously inaccessible habitat for salmon. It also addressed cultural resources and maintained a dependable source of clean water for Bellingham.The project brought together a number of organisations, including American Rivers, the Nooksack Indian Tribe, the Lummi Nation and the City of Bellingham, alongside private funding from the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation and other partners.Dam removals across the US reopened rivers and restored vital fish habitatIn New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest, a 21-foot concrete and earth dam once blocked the South Branch Gale River after being built in 1955 by the Littleton Water and Light Department as part of a water-supply system. By 2020, the dam was no longer in use, and its removal restored connectivity to about 15 miles of river upstream and 21 miles downstream.In South Carolina, the Burson Lake Dam on Reedy Creek faced a different problem after heavy rainfall damaged its spillway in spring 2020, increasing the risk of failure; rather than repair the ageing recreation dam, the US Forest Service chose to remove it, eliminating a safety concern and future maintenance costs while restoring habitat for aquatic species such as Bartram’s bass. In Indiana, the Elkhart River Dam, built around 1890 to divert water into raceways that once powered downtown industry, had outlived its original purpose but continued to block fish passage; removing the roughly eight-foot structure reconnected about 40 miles of upstream habitat and was expected to benefit 16 fish species and improve movement and genetic mixing among about 50 species, including the threatened or endangered greater redhorse, longnose dace and northern brook lamprey.In Montana, removal of the more than century-old Rattlesnake Creek Dam reconnected the Rattlesnake Wilderness with the Clark Fork River, while restoration plans included removing other structures, restoring about 1,000 feet of stream channel and creating five acres of wetland and floodplain habitat. On Washington’s Pilchuck River, two diversion dams were removed by the Tulalip Tribes and City of Snohomish, opening more than 36 miles of upstream habitat for Chinook, coho, chum and pink salmon, steelhead, bull trout, cutthroat trout and other species, while also reducing dam-failure risks and improving recreational opportunities.The wider impact of 69 US dam removals in 2020The 69 dam removals in 2020 were small compared with major US dams, but together they reconnected 624 miles of river. They restored fish passage in some areas while removing redundant or unsafe infrastructure in others.The wider debate includes larger proposals, such as Congressman Mike Simpson’s 2021 plan to remove four lower Snake River dams as part of a broader strategy involving salmon, energy, agriculture and regional infrastructure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: HYDERABAD: Days before minister Konda Surekha was sacked from the Cabinet, she was seen tying a rakhi to chief minister A Revanth Reddy at his residen.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: Days before minister Konda Surekha was sacked from the Cabinet, she was seen tying a rakhi to chief minister A Revanth Reddy at his residence, amid a controversy over remarks made by her daughter against the CM and the Congress party.In the video, Surekha, along with Women and Child Welfare Minister Seethakka, is seen tying a rakhi to Revanth Reddy during Raksha Bandhan celebrations.After the celebrations, Revanth posted on X: “On the occasion of Raksha Bandhan, which stands as a symbol of the bond between sisters and brothers, ministers Seethakka and Konda Surekha tied rakhis. I wish that this Raksha Bandhan festival brings joy to every girl child. #RakshaBandhan #Rakhi #Telangana.”In a separate post, he said: “To every elder sister, younger sister. People’s governance is Rakshabandhan. #RakshaBandhan #Rakhi #Telangana.”Speaking to reporters, Surekha said she had tied a rakhi to Revanth as she had done over the past two years.Asked about demands from Congress legislators for action against her, she said: “I do not want to comment on this auspicious festive day.”She added that she had prayed for the blessings of women to remain with Revanth.“Don’t single me out in this case. Today is a festival day and we all women have tied rakhis to the CM,” she said.Controversy over daughter’s remarksThe Raksha Bandhan celebrations came amid a controversy over remarks made by Surekha’s daughter, Konda Susmita, against Revanth and the Congress party.Susmita had criticised Revanth after he stated that sitting Parkal MLA Revuri Prakash Reddy would be given the Congress ticket from the constituency in the next Assembly election.A contender for the ticket herself, Susmita had said on August 19 that the CM did not have the authority to make such a decision and had also levelled other allegations against him.Surekha maintained that she could not be held responsible for her adult daughter’s comments. articles.title: Seatbelt sign off, hydraulic failure, pilot tests positive for psychoactive substance: What Air India Phuket probe found
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has provided a detailed account of the August 4 incident involvin.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A preliminary report by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has provided a detailed account of the August 4 incident involving Air India flight AI-2379 from Phuket to Delhi.The report examines the pilots' post-flight medical tests, a series of hydraulic-system failures, the aircraft's sudden altitude upset, the response of the flight crew, injuries caused inside the cabin and damage to the aircraft.Here are the key points that are covered in the report.Pilot's psycho-active substance test: Both pilots underwent post-flight medical checks after the aircraft landed in Delhi. Their breath analyser tests were satisfactory. However, a psycho-active substance detection test found the Pilot-In-Command's sample to be non-negative. His blood sample was subsequently sent for confirmatory testing, which was also found to be non-negative. The co-pilot tested negative in both tests.What triggered the incident: The aircraft was cruising at FL360, or about 36,000 feet, when its flight-control system detected a loss of pressure in the green hydraulic system at 04:02:43 UTC. Four seconds later, it detected the loss of the blue and yellow hydraulic systems too.Autopilot disengaged: At 04:02:48 UTC, the aircraft's autopilot disengaged, and a continuous repetitive chime sounded. Three seconds later, a stall warning was triggered for two seconds.Aircraft suddenly moved away from its assigned altitude: The co-pilot, who was the pilot flying, initially responded to the situation. The pilot-in-command then took over the controls. During the altitude upset, the aircraft gained 372 feet and then fell 292 feet from its assigned FL360.Hydraulic systems recovered: The blue hydraulic system recovered at around 04:02:52 UTC. The yellow and green systems recovered a few seconds later. The recovery restored the flight-control surfaces, and the aircraft returned to normal operating condition.Why passengers were injured: The aircraft was cruising at FL360 when the altitude upset occurred and, crucially, the seat-belt signs were off. The sudden movement resulted in injuries to passengers and cabin crew. The cabin supervisor informed the cockpit about the injuries.24 people needed medical attention: On landing in Delhi, the airport medical team treated 20 passengers and four cabin crew members. Twenty were discharged after initial treatment for minor injuries, while four people with serious injuries were hospitalised for further treatment.Crew chose to continue to Delhi: After assessing the cabin situation, the flight crew decided not to divert to the nearest en-route airport and continued towards Delhi. They later requested medical priority from Delhi ATC. The aircraft landed safely at IGI Airport at 05:30 UTC.Aircraft suffered cabin damage: The altitude upset also caused damage inside the aircraft. The report records cracked and deformed ceiling panels, dislocated passenger-service-unit panels, broken handrails, damaged emergency-exit hardware and dislodged overhead-bin doors. An overhead-bin divider was cracked, a lavatory commode was uprooted, a crew seat was bent, and panels around the rear crew-door area were severely damaged.Hydraulic failure being investigated: The A320 has three hydraulic systems, known as green, blue and yellow. The systems provide hydraulic power to major aircraft systems. AAIB has removed relevant hydraulic components and collected hydraulic samples for further analysis.Warnings recorded after the flight: The aircraft's post flight report recorded a sequence of warnings including "HYD GREEN SYS LO PR", followed by blue and yellow hydraulic warnings. It also recorded "AUTO FLT AP OFF" and an elevator fault.Aircraft had an existing MEL item: Before departing Phuket, maintenance personnel found no discrepancies other than an already invoked minimum equipment list (MEL) item. The aircraft had been dispatched under MEL item 29-23-01A, relating to the power transfer unit (PTU), which had been invoked on July 28. The crew's walk-around inspection found no discrepancies.No adverse weather reported: Despite the incident initially being notified as a turbulence encounter, the report says no adverse weather was reported by either the flight crew or ATC during the altitude upset.Experienced pilot-in-command: The 34-year-old PIC held a valid ATPL and had 5,055 hours of total flying experience, all recorded on the aircraft type. He had flown the type on August 3, the day before the incident. His recorded rest period before the flight was 21 hours and 59 minutes.Co-pilot was flying when the event began: The 32-year-old co-pilot held a valid CPL and had 1,393 hours of flying experience. The report identifies him as the pilot flying during the incident, while the PIC was the pilot monitoring before taking over the controls.AAIB calls finding a serious concern: The report says, "The confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern, and AAIB recommends appropriate actions by DGCA on priority." It separately recommends that the DGCA take appropriate measures to prevent abuse of psycho-active substances.Flight recorders are being examined: Both the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder were recovered. Their downloaded data is now with the investigation team for analysis.Airbus experts examined the aircraft: Technical experts assigned by France's BEA, including Airbus experts, inspected the aircraft from August 13 to 15. Hydraulic components and samples were subsequently collected for testing.AAIB says the detailed investigation into the technical and other aspects is still underway. Maintenance and operational records, fuel and oil samples, ATC data and flight-recorder information are among the material being examined.The preliminary report records both the hydraulic-system failures and the PIC's non-negative confirmatory psycho-active substance test, but it does not establish that the substance finding caused the altitude upset. AAIB says the investigation remains in progress and that a final report will be published later.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Protein and creatine never delivered; customer gets refund plus Rs 50,000 compensation
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The district consumer commission in Himachal Pradesh has directed Muscle Beast to refund Rs 7,875 to a customer who paid for protein and cr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The district consumer commission in Himachal Pradesh has directed Muscle Beast to refund Rs 7,875 to a customer who paid for protein and creatine supplements online but never received the products. The commission also awarded Rs 30,000 for mental tension and harassment and Rs 20,000 towards litigation expenses. The order was passed on August 24, 2026.Why did the customer approach the commission?According to the commission order, Davesh Duvedi booked protein powder and creatine monohydrate powder supplements from Muscle Beast through an online purchase on June 11, 2022. He paid Rs 7,875 through UPI and was assured that the consignment would be delivered within seven days.However, the products were not delivered within the promised period. When Duvedi contacted the company, he was assured that the delivery would be made within another one or two days. After 15 days, he contacted the company again and was given similar assurances.The company eventually refused to deliver the products, according to the complaint. Duvedi alleged that the company neither supplied the products nor returned his money, causing him financial loss and mental harassment.The company did not appear before the commission and was proceeded against ex-parte. Duvedi then produced his affidavit and payment receipt in support of his complaint.Why did the commission rule in the customer's favour?The bench comprising President D.R. Thakur and members Minakshi Rana and Anoop Kumar found that the payment of Rs 7,875 had been established through the receipt. It also noted that the products were neither delivered nor was the amount refunded despite requests."Complainant in order to prove his case has produced his affidavit Annexure C-1 and receipt Annexure C-2. As per complainant, he has booked the articles i.e. Protein Power and Creatine Monohydrate Power Supplements through online purchase from opposite party and paid Rupees 7875/- to opposite party online. But no any article was given to complainant nor any amount was given back despite request," the commission said.The bench noted that Duvedi had also proved that the company had promised delivery within seven days but failed to fulfil that assurance. It held that retaining the payment without delivering the products or returning the money amounted to deficiency in service."Complainant has proved this fact that opposite party has taken amount of Rupees 7875/- from him but despite request made by complainant neither opposite parties had delivered the article nor had paid back the amount of Rupees 7875/- to complainant which is deficiency in service on behalf of opposite party and therefore complainant is entitled to the claim," it further said.The commission allowed the complaint and directed Muscle Beast to refund Rs 7,875 with 9 percent annual interest from the date of filing of the complaint. It also awarded Rs 30,000 for mental tension and harassment and Rs 20,000 towards litigation expenses.The refund and other amounts have to be paid within 30 days of receipt of a copy of the order.

articles.title: In 1875, a one-room schoolhouse taught generations of American children; 151 years later, it was donated to a nonprofit as a new restoration fight begins
articles.summary: US News: A historic one-room schoolhouse built in 1875 is entering a new chapter in Delaware County, Indiana, after surviving closure, storm damage, neglect an.
articles.body: A historic one-room schoolhouse built in 1875 is entering a new chapter in Delaware County, Indiana, after surviving closure, storm damage, neglect and an earlier rescue from possible demolition. Schoolhouse No. 3, also known as the ‘Corinth schoolhouse,’ once served rural children before closing after the 1912–13 school year. More than a century later, the building has again begun to show the effects of age, prompting a newly formed nonprofit to step in. In August 2026, the family of the late ‘Dr Norman and Hermie Miller’ officially donated the property to One Room Schoolhouse No. 3, Inc.(a non-profit organization in Muncie, Indiana, formed to preserve and restore the historic 1875 Corinth Schoolhouse), giving the organisation responsibility for its future. Now, 151 years after the schoolhouse was built, another fight to protect this small but remarkable piece of local history is underway.Why does the 151-year-old Corinth schoolhouse need restoration workAccording to the Ted Shideler blog, the restoration became necessary as the 151-year-old schoolhouse showed increasing signs of deterioration. It is one of Delaware County's treasured historic landmarks which faced serious threats in the past, and time had once again begun to take its toll. The building required a new roof, a reconstructed cupola, tuckpointing and other structural repairs. Its condition had also worsened enough to force the suspension of educational field trips, cutting off one of the ways the historic schoolhouse had continued to serve the community.The restoration effort, therefore, is about far more than improving the appearance of an old building. Its immediate purpose is to stabilise and protect the structure before further damage makes preservation even more difficult. In order to do that, the nonprofit's first fundraising campaign originally set a goal of $52,000. Supporters eventually exceeded that target, allowing restoration work to begin in September 2026, according to the Muncie Journal.The early history of the Corinth schoolhouseThe history of the present-day Corinth schoolhouse goes back further than the brick building that still stands today. According to Ted Shideler's blog, the first school in Monroe Township was established during the winter of 1830–31. As the township grew, it was divided into several school districts, with each district having its own local school. The area served by what became District No. 3, originally had a school located about a mile south of the present Corinth schoolhouse. A frame school was probably built on the current site in 1874, before the existing brick one-room schoolhouse was constructed there in 1875. This building, known as Schoolhouse No. 3 or the Corinth schoolhouse, educated local children until it closed after the 1912–13 school year, when its pupils were transferred to the school in Cowan. The old schoolhouse was later used by farmers to store animals and equipment, but the building itself survived long after its days as a classroom had ended.How was the historic schoolhouse saved from an uncertain futureThe building's first major modern rescue came after a 1991 windstorm caused damage. According to the Shideler blog, Eleanor Miller and Helen Ross donated the schoolhouse to the ‘Delaware County Historical Society’ a year later. Various plans for its future were considered, but little came from them. Eventually, ‘Norman Miller’ took the lead in restoring the building alongside the Delaware County ‘Retired Teachers Association.’ His connection to the schoolhouse was personal because his father, Perry Miller, had once attended classes there.The restoration gave the building a new roof and cupola and added period-correct furniture from around 1900. The schoolhouse was then used as a living history museum, allowing local 4th-grade pupils to experience the environment in which earlier generations had learned. The Muncie Journal reported that Norman Miller and his wife, Hermie, had also recognised the building's importance when it faced possible collapse and demolition. Working with family members and others in the community, they helped ensure that it remained standing.The Miller family passes the schoolhouse on to a new generation of caretakersFollowing Norman Miller's death, his children began looking for a way to protect the schoolhouse permanently. The Muncie Journal reported that they eventually found a connection with ‘Colleen Cooper,’ whose vision was to create a nonprofit dedicated not only to preserving the building but also to turning it into a place for education and community activity. That idea led to the formation of One Room Schoolhouse No. 3, Inc. Its mission is to preserve the historic structure while developing educational experiences and programmes for people of different ages.In August, the Miller family officially donated the schoolhouse to the organisation. Birgie Miller Gresham, representing the family, announced the decision during a donor appreciation event. For the family, the donation represents a continuation of the commitment begun by Norman and Hermie Miller. The building is no longer simply being maintained by one family; its future has now been placed in the hands of a wider community organisation.What could the restored Corinth schoolhouse offer the communityRestoration is only the beginning of the nonprofit's plans. According to the Muncie Journal, future ambitions include bringing back educational field trips, history programmes, workshops, community events and partnerships with schools and other organisations. That would return the building to the role it once played in local life. Instead of being a forgotten structure, it could again become a place where people gather to learn. Although many old one-room schools still survive across Indiana, most have been heavily altered, abandoned or converted for entirely different purposes, as per the Shideler blog. Schoolhouse No. 3 remains recognisable as a 19th-century rural schoolhouse. The latest donation and fundraising success have created a chance for it to begin again. The small brick building’s next challenge will be ensuring that the future generations can still walk through its doors and understand the stories held within its walls.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Grumpy Old Men star Walter Matthau and his wife gave a Roxbury hayfield to a land trust in 1997; nearly 30 years later, the Connecticut preserve still keeps its views open
articles.summary: US News: Actor Walter Matthau donated 32 acres of hayfield in Roxbury, Connecticut, to a land trust in 1997. Almost three decades later, the preserve remains an active farm, ensuring open views and local agriculture thrive. Discover how a small donation can have a lasting impact.
articles.body: Most of Walter Matthau’s acting career was devoted to creating the image of a grumpy old man in his numerous films together with Jack Lemmon, most notably in “Grumpy Old Men.” But in a quiet little town of Roxbury, Connecticut, in Litchfield County, he made a rather inconspicuous decision that was not related to anything funny at all. He gave away one of his hayfields to a local land trust to preserve it from development forever. It is an example of how an ordinary donation of a property can withstand the test of time for many decades.The 1997 donation to the Roxbury Land TrustThe piece of land was donated to the Roxbury Land Trust by Matthau and his wife Carole in 1997, based on a description of the property from the land trust itself, which states that the piece of land is an active hayfield with open scenic views of the east side, as per the official site of the organization at Matthau Preserve. The land trust's own materials give slightly different acreage figures for the property: the Matthau Preserve page lists it at 32 acres, while the trust's historical timeline records the 1997 donation as a 34-acre preserve. In either case, the land is one of the medium-sized preserves owned by the trust.In fact, Roxbury has always been known to attract writers, actors and artists in search of isolation close to New York City and Matthau was among several such distinguished inhabitants who contributed their lands to this conservation effort. William and Rose Styron added their 22 acres of land to the trust in the same year, thus creating the Styron Preserve in the neighborhood of the Matthau land, an act that has been recorded in the trust's organizational history. The Styron Preserve, together with the 27-acre Widmark Preserve and a small connecting parcel, forms part of a chain of protected land that stretches all the way to the 467-acre Good Hill Farm Preserve, a corridor totaling roughly 800 acres in all.Why an active hayfield matters more than an abandoned field Contrary to the preserve’s wild growth pattern, the Matthau Preserve remains a hayfield in full operation. That is exactly the purpose for which the New England land trusts seek to keep donated farmland in active agricultural use rather than allowing it to return to forest, because mowing hayfields not only keeps the rural landscape viewable through its open vistas, but also sustains low-level agriculture needed for local hay production. It is that exact combination that allows the preserve to maintain its view to the east after almost three decades since its donation, instead of letting it be covered with trees that will naturally reclaim uncultivated land.The Roxbury Land Trust was established in 1970 and currently manages more than 30 preserves totaling roughly 4,000 acres, interconnected through a series of hiking trails. Though the Matthau Preserve takes up only a tiny part of the land managed by the trust, its location within the group of several more celebrity-donated preserves along Tophet Road shows how much the land trust depends on donations.A career built on comic timing and a different kind of legacyMatthau’s success was solely dependent on his performance in front of a camera. Born in New York City on October 1, 1920, Matthau built his entire career around his signature gravelly voice and hangdog demeanor, states his Encyclopædia Britannica biography. He received an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for his role in “The Fortune Cookie” at the 39th Academy Awards ceremony in 1967 for movies that were released in 1966. He passed away on July 1, 2000, in Santa Monica, California, aged 79, spending his latter years playing mostly comedy parts.The preserve's enduring open views and working hayfield are thanks to the agreement Matthau made back in 1997, rather than to anything he did in a studio. In general, once the land has been passed over to a nonprofit trust whose goal is conservation, the deed is always accompanied by some sort of restriction, meaning that neither the trust nor any other owner in the future will be able to sell the land to developers. And the history of the Roxbury Land Trust proves it time and again.A small gift with a long shelf lifeThe donation’s significance is not its size. It is small in comparison to other donations, such as the 467-acre Good Hill Farm Preserve and the 360-acre Mine Hill Preserve. What is significant about the Matthau donation is just how little maintenance it needs to provide its benefit continuously. Once the property is donated, the eastern views and hayfield nature that made it worthy of being donated will continue with minimal maintenance, no action from Matthau's family and no fear of the land being subdivided into housing parcels.Almost three decades since a comedic actor famous for bickering with his friends throughout his twilight years in movies made an unspectacular decision regarding a farm in Connecticut, that decision is working perfectly fine in providing exactly what it was meant to provide: the hayfield gets mowed and the views remain open.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: From 2019 to 2023, a tech entrepreneur spent $19.125 million assembling a 31.5-acre Martha’s Vineyard estate; in 2026 it sold for a Massachusetts-record $43 million
articles.summary: News News: A property in Edgartown on Martha’s Vineyard has sold for $43 million, setting a new real estate record for both the island and Massachusetts. The est.
articles.body: A property in Edgartown on Martha’s Vineyard has sold for $43 million, setting a new real estate record for both the island and Massachusetts. The estate, known as Great Point, covers 31.59 acres and includes an 8,994-square-foot home with 12 bedrooms.The property is located at 15 Forever Wild Way in Edgartown, facing the South Coast of Martha’s Vineyard and near Edgartown Great Pond. According to the Wall Street Journal, it was listed for $49 million in June before selling for $43 million.The seller was Michael Bronner, a Boston-based technology entrepreneur and investor. Bronner spent $19.125 million between 2019 and 2023 to assemble the property. The buyer has not been identified.The sale also stands out because Great Point has surpassed the previous Martha’s Vineyard record of $37.5 million, set by a Katama mansion that sold last year. It also beat the Massachusetts record of $38.1 million, set in 2023 when the Nantucket waterfront property Beams End was sold.Record-breaking saleGreat Point is located within the Herring Creek Farm area of Edgartown, where neighbouring properties are owned by high-profile people including David Letterman. The estate’s large size and location make it part of the high-value property market that has continued to attract attention on Martha’s Vineyard.The previous island record was held by a Katama mansion that sold for $37.5 million. The property was described as being inspired by 'The Great Gatsby' and was sold to Witchwood Lane Trust. It was also part of the portfolio of Vineyard architect Patrick Ahearn.Great Point’s $43 million sale has now pushed that record higher. It has also moved past the Massachusetts record held by Beams End, a waterfront property on Nantucket that sold for $38.1 million in 2023.The record sale comes as the wider Martha’s Vineyard property market is seeing fewer transactions but more money being spent on high-value homes.More money at top end of marketA 2026 mid-year market report by Tea Lane Associates found that the number of property transactions fell by 5 per cent in the first half of the year. There were 148 transactions, compared with 155 during the same period in 2025.Despite the fall in transactions, the total dollar value of sales rose by 23 per cent, from $304 million in the first half of 2025 to $375 million in the first half of 2026.The average price of a property sale also increased by 29 per cent, rising from $1.96 million to $2.53 million. The report said this was the highest average price recorded for the first half of a year.“This is the highest average price for the first half of the year ever, blowing past the last peak of first half average price which occurred in the first half of 2023 where the average transaction price was $2.061 million,” the report said.The number of high-value sales also increased. There were 12 sales above $5 million in the first half of 2026, compared with seven during the first half of 2025. Sales above $10 million rose from one to six.Tea Lane Associates also found that properties selling for more than $3 million made up 21 per cent of all transactions in the first half of 2026. They accounted for 55 per cent of the total dollar volume. During the same period in 2025, such properties represented 17 per cent of transactions and 44 per cent of dollar volume.High-end homes and housing problemEdgartown was the most active area for real estate transactions in 2025, accounting for 32 per cent of transactions and 45 per cent of the dollar volume, according to Tea Lane Associates.The growing value of luxury properties has also drawn attention because housing affordability remains a major issue on Martha’s Vineyard. The Tea Lane report was discussed with US Senator Elizabeth Warren during her visit to the island last month.Warren spoke about the challenges created by increasing wealth among billionaires and said communities would need to find creative ways to deal with the housing shortage. One example she gave was turning abandoned buildings into homes instead of relying only on building more housing.“I understand why they’d want to come here, but preserving an economy that works under those circumstances has gotten about 10 times harder,” Warren said about wealthy people coming to the island.Tom Wallace, principal broker of Wallace & Co. Sotheby’s International Realty, previously said the market was showing growing demand for family compounds.“This property reflects a movement toward a desire for not just a home, but a family compound. And it is an appetite for this kind of property that is ever increasing, and very appealing,” Wallace said in June.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: A $5.5M Portland power project could remove 400 trees from Forest Park while powering over 55,000 homes; the deal has split conservation groups
articles.summary: US News: Portland General Electric's Harborton Reliability Project, which would cut down 400 trees on a 5-acre plot, is facing massive backlash from conservati.
articles.body: Portland General Electric's Harborton Reliability Project, which would cut down 400 trees on a 5-acre plot, is facing massive backlash from conservation groups. While the project is yet to gain final approval from City Hall, it is already facing contention.According to a report by Ecoticias.com, the project is vital to maintain reliable power for over 55,000 homes and businesses. However, detractors argue that mature forest, wetlands, waterways, and wildlife will suffer the brunt. The city is awaiting a staff report recommending the revised application.Why the project mattersAccording to PGE, a new 1,400 ft segment of high-voltage transmission line would improve distribution of electricity in the event of equipment failure or spikes in demand during extreme heat waves or cold spells. It would also include an upgrade to a decades-old line inside a utility corridor. The utility points to potential outages in parts of Portland coming as soon as 2028 if the work is not approved.Initially, it was agreed that PGE would funnel $5.5 million into habitat restoration in and around Forest Park in addition to environmental remediation needed after the construction is finished. The money could fund wetland restoration and wildfire fuel reduction along with land and wildlife conservation and invasive plant removal. However, the final decision over the allocation of funds will be made by the city.Once the agreement features a revised construction plan and more technical analysis, a public hearing must be held before an officer whose decision can be subject to an appeals process with City Council. The proposal also allotted $250,000 for an outside consultant to evaluate feasibility.Why the critics are calling it a bad dealForest Park Conservancy, Bird Alliance of Oregon and Forest Park Neighbourhood Association were not at all satisfied with the mediation process. They refused to sign the agreement after being excluded from final negotiations, which they described as a “backroom agreement” that circumvented legitimate public review.They called for $7.5 million, $2 million more than PGE’s offer, placing $5 million of that into a conservation trust for better public oversight. Their plan asks for restoration of up to 100 acres in the park’s north end to compensate for forest damage, clean up streams, and restore habitat connectivity.As of now, the trees are safe. The city must still review PGE's revised application, publish notice, schedule a hearing and hear the independent auditor. Although recent developments lean towards approval of the agreement, the ecological cost still has to be weighed in a public, transparent process with all concerned parties included.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: LUCKNOW: The Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) operational unit in Lucknow has arrested six active drug traffickers and recovered a large consignment of narcotic and psychotropic medicines, including codeine-based cough syrup, tramadol capsules, and alprazolam tablets, collectively valued at an estimated Rs 1 crore.The arrests were made on Friday at Kanhaiya Pharma in Transport Nagar, Lucknow.Kishan Vaswani, Sameer Ahmed, Shad Irshad, Umesh Kumar, Satendra Singh, and Vishal Chaurasia were arrested.According to the ANTF, the accused were found in possession of 720 bottles of 100-ml ONEREX cough syrup containing codeine, 1,20,000 SPASMONAM PLUS capsules containing Tramadol Hydrochloride, and 9,60,000 ALZOMAC-0.5 tablets containing Alprazolam.Besides the drugs, the team also recovered seven mobile phones and Rs 11,140 in cash from the suspects.A case has been registered at Sarojini Nagar police station in the Lucknow Commissionerate under Sections 8, 21, 22, and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Police said legal proceedings have been initiated against all six accused.During interrogation, the arrested suspects reportedly told investigators that they operated together to illegally procure and sell narcotic medicines for higher profits.They allegedly pooled money to purchase the medicines and subsequently delivered the consignments to different parties for monetary gain. The money earned from the transactions was then divided among the members of the group and used for their personal expenses and lifestyles, police said.Investigators said the questioning of the accused had yielded important information regarding the suspected drug network. The ANTF is now working on the forward and backward linkages of the case to identify the source from which the medicines were procured, the intended recipients of the consignment, and other persons associated with the network.Further investigation is underway to establish the complete supply chain and identify other individuals involved in the illegal trade.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: WhatsApp group, engineers and a race against time: How 2 workers were rescued from Nepal tunnel
articles.summary: South Asia News: The operation at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project was a painstaking process. It began with simply reaching the buried tunnel and eventually in.
articles.body: The operation at the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower project was a painstaking process. It began with simply reaching the buried tunnel and eventually involved excavators, oxygen pipes, technical drawings, former plant employees, engineers and specialists advising rescuers in real time.Two hydropower workers were pulled alive from a debris-buried tunnel in Nepal on Friday, nine days after a catastrophic flood swept through the Trishuli valley. Their rescue offered a rare breakthrough on the tenth day of efforts that had repeatedly been stalled by huge volumes of mud, rocks and debris.The Nepali Army shared a snippet from the rescue operation that saved the two tunnel workers. In a video that has now garnered over 17k views show the workers crawling in and then pulling out a tunnel worker successfully. Calling the event "miraculous" the army said that the two workers got their rebirth after 10 days."After 10 Days of Intense Struggle—Rebirth of Two Lives, a Miraculous Victory of Hope. Trishuli 3A. Two People Rescued Alive from the Tunnel," it wrote.How the rescue operation was carried outStep 1: Rescuers first had to reach the buried tunnelThe August 26 flood had completely transformed the landscape around the hydropower projects. A huge wall of water, mud and rock, triggered by a vast glacial and rock collapse on a mountain on the China-Nepal border, buried tunnel entrances and altered the terrain around them.At Upper Trishuli 3A, rescuers took almost six days just to reach the tunnel because its entrance had been buried.The problem was not simply a blocked entrance. “This is not a normal closure of tunnels,” Nepal Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said. He added that the flood had changed the terrain around the tunnels and altered their structure, while mud, rocks, soil and other debris had accumulated inside.Step 2: Heavy machinery began clearing the wayOnce rescuers reached the site, excavators were used to move huge boulders and debris from the mouth of the tunnel.Excavators were attempting to clear the tunnel entrance and work their way deeper inside, as reported by news agency Reuters, citing a photographer who flew over the site.The teams were effectively fighting their way through a newly created underground blockage rather than entering an intact tunnel.Step 3: Rescuers tried to keep anyone trapped inside aliveEven before reaching possible survivors, teams were preparing for the possibility that people remained alive inside cavities.At Upper Trishuli 3A, rescuers had been trying to supply oxygen through pipes into cavities where someone might have been trapped.At other sites, the same question was being asked: if workers had survived the initial flood and reached a chamber, could they still have access to food and water?At Rasuwagadhi, rescuers reached 250 metres into one tunnel before finding it blocked. Officials said as many as 46 people might have been trapped in a chamber where they could potentially have access to food and water.Step 4: Engineers turned WhatsApp into a rescue toolAs physical access became difficult, technical knowledge became just as important as machinery.An engineers' WhatsApp group, created before the disaster, became a real-time support network for the rescue operation. It was expanded to include more experts and eventually had more than 500 members. Officials and rescue workers used the group to obtain information about the underground tunnel networks.At Chilime, for instance, a government official posted, “Can you send me Chilime layout drawings.” Minutes later, a member of the group responded with drawings of the project's powerhouse and details of its access tunnels.The rescue teams also sought advice from former plant employees, whose knowledge of the tunnel networks helped them understand how to approach the buried structures.Step 5: Missing workers' phone numbers were also circulatedThe engineers' group was used for another possible avenue of locating survivors.Members shared the names and mobile phone numbers of missing workers, asking government officials to pass the information to telecom authorities in an attempt to establish their last recorded locations.Step 6: Rescuers searched for a response from insideAt Upper Trishuli 3A, the breakthrough came after days of digging.Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix, who had been supporting the operation remotely, said teams had cleared approximately 50 to 60 metres (164–196 feet) of debris blocking the tunnel.Earlier on Friday, Dix said rescuers believed they had heard a faint response from inside. He said the response was reportedly “hunchha”, meaning “yes” or “OK”. Rescuers had called into the tunnel, “Don't worry, we are rescuing you.”The faint response gave the teams a possible sign that someone was still alive.Step 7: Breakthrough in less than an hour laterThe teams had been hoping for a breakthrough at any moment.Less than an hour after Dix described the faint response, rescuers pulled the two men out alive.The two workers were identified as Sanjay Shah (30), a mechanical foreman and Kabir Maharjan, (45), a mechanical supervisorStep 8: The workers were brought out through the muddy openingThe extraction itself was arduous.One worker emerged through a muddy opening. Rescuers helped him to his feet before carrying him on their backs towards a helicopter. He raised his hand as the emergency workers took him away.The second man emerged caked in mud and was carried away on a stretcher, with photographs showing his hands pressed together in prayer. Both men were subsequently taken for medical treatment.The Nepal Army said the search-and-rescue operation was continuing.An international and expert-backed rescue effortNepali rescuers were supported by experts from India, China and South Korea.Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, was supporting the operation remotely and said the rescue was “back in miracle country” after what he described as a “week of 24/7 heartache”.Dix had also been a key adviser during the 2023 Himalayan rescue operation that freed all 41 Indian workers trapped inside a collapsed under-construction road tunnel.Wider search: More tunnels, more blockagesThe rescue of Shah and Maharjan was the first confirmed sign that tunnel workers had survived the disaster. Authorities had initially believed that more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels. Rescuers were continuing searches at Upper Trishuli 3A and other sites.At Rasuwagadhi, teams had already penetrated 250 metres before being blocked. They were planning to go inside again.At Chilime, the Independent Power Producers' Association said at least eight people could be trapped, while a Nepal Electricity Authority official said 46 may be trapped at Rasuwagadhi.Why the tunnel searches were so difficultThe flood deposited an estimated 2.2 million tonnes of mud and debris down the valley. This meant that even locating tunnel entrances became difficult. At Chilime, Reuters reported a large tunnel entrance with flood debris rising to the ceiling a short way inside.Across the valley, rescuers repeatedly encountered walls of hard-packed debris.The disaster behind the rescueThe floods followed a huge glacial and rock collapse on August 26, unleashing what Nepal's foreign minister called a “Himalayan tsunami”.The resulting floods tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and multiple hydropower dams. At least 12 hydropower projects were smashed, while the disaster wiped out around 10% of Nepal's generation capacity.Rescue workers were searching six hydroelectric sites in the valley, at least three of which were under construction.Survivors who escaped before the flood buried the plantsAt Upper Trishuli 1, civil engineer Jan Jiwan Thakur said a colleague warned him about the approaching flood moments before it swept down the valley.He and around 100 others from the facility ran towards higher ground. “We just ran away towards the hillside and, after two to three minutes, when we looked down, everything was gone,” Thakur said. He said the flood debris had completely covered their office area.Another survivor, Dhan Bahadur Tamang, described escaping through a tunnel as the flood struck. Pipes and other equipment were swept inside, but his knowledge of the tunnel system helped him and others find a way out. He said he saw dead bodies during the underground escape.Families still waitingAs the rescue operation continued, some families had begun holding symbolic funerals for missing relatives as hopes of finding survivors faded. Among those still waiting was Rajesh Shrestha, whose 30-year-old son Rajish, an environmental engineer at Upper Trishuli 1, remained missing.“Whenever I look outside, I imagine seeing him carrying a bag and coming home, just as he used to,” Shrestha said, “I am surviving on the hope that he will return.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A popular DM, a sudden exit, an unanswered question
articles.summary: Today, I voluntarily resigned from the IAS, bringing an unforgettable 13-year journey to a close.” With those words, Divya Mittal announced on social .
articles.body: Today, I voluntarily resigned from the IAS, bringing an unforgettable 13-year journey to a close.” With those words, Divya Mittal announced on social media on Sunday that she was walking away from the civil services. The resignation of the 43-year-old, 2013-batch Uttar Pradesh-cadre officer, who was serving as special secretary in the revenue department, is yet to be formally accepted.Mittal has not disclosed why she quit, telling TOI that she will reveal her plans at the appropriate time. Her farewell post instead retraced her journey from IIT-Delhi and IIM-Bangalore to a job in London, and then back to India to repay what she called a “debt to this soil”.Why Her Exit Stunned ManyHer decision surprised colleagues and admirers because Mittal had acquired a public following unusual for a bureaucrat. In Mirzapur and Deoria, she became known as an accessible, hands-on administrator who used social media to communicate her work.Her best-known initiative brought piped water to Lahuriya Deh, a remote hilltop hamlet whose residents had long depended on tankers and water collected from pits. In her farewell note, Mittal recalled an elderly woman silently touching her head and blessing her when water reached the village.Village representatives also remember “Mera Gaon, Mera Gaurav”, a WhatsApp group connecting more than 800 pradhans with district officials. Mittal would tag officials when problems were raised and monitor the response, effectively giving village heads a direct line to the administration.Popular, but sometimes at oddsThose who worked with her describe two distinct sides to her administrative personality. She was soft-spoken and approachable with members of the public, but could lose her temper in official meetings when instructions were ignored. Her willingness to take decisions independently won her admirers, but it did not always make for easy relations with elected representatives.The completion of the Lahuriya Deh water project itself became a source of friction. Mittal performed the “jal puja” when water reached the village, but elected representatives were absent. Critics accused her of sidelining politicians; her supporters saw an administrator more interested in finishing the work than managing political optics.She was transferred from Mirzapur soon after the event and remained without a posting for several months.There had been confrontations earlier, too. During her tenure as Sant Kabir Nagar DM, Mittal found herself at odds with then district minister-in-charge Ashish Patel, husband of Union minister and Mirzapur MP Anupriya Patel, after she sent a representative to receive him instead of attending personally. As Deoria DM, differences during a District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee meeting also generated controversy.Her visibility added another layer to the friction. In Deoria, she came to be known as the “reel wali DM” due to her frequent social-media posts on govt initiatives, community events and public outreach. Supporters saw it as an effort to make the administration more accessible. Detractors questioned whether the officer’s public profile was beginning to overshadow the institution she represented.From London to the IASSuch attention was far removed from the circumstances in which Mittal grew up. Born in Rewari, Haryana, she was raised in a modest household before her family moved to Delhi, which is listed as her home district in civil-service records.She studied engineering at IIT-Delhi between 2001 and 2005 and then attended IIM-Bangalore. After completing her management degree, she joined JPMorgan in London.Her husband, Gagandeep Singh Dhillon, had travelled much the same route a few years before her. He was Mittal’s senior at both IIT-Delhi and IIM-Bangalore and subsequently worked with Citigroup in London. The couple married in April 2007 and began their corporate careers in the UK.Despite well-paying jobs in international finance, they jointly decided to return to India in 2009 and prepare for the civil services. Mittal eventually joined the IAS in 2013. Dhillon entered the Indian Trade Service in 2011 and worked in areas including foreign trade and export controls.The parallel between their careers did not end there. In May 2022, Dhillon resigned from govt service and returned to financial markets. He now works as an algorithmic trader at Neuracap, according to his LinkedIn profile. Four years later, Mittal has followed him out of the civil services, although she has given no indication that she intends to return to finance.Former colleagues say Mittal’s ambition and appetite for difficult assignments were evident early in her career. Her batchmate Sunil Kumar Verma recalls that when delays arose in cadre allocation at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration, Mittal and two other officers took on the technically demanding exercise themselves and completed it for the entire batch.Did she hit a plateau?Some senior officers who know her describe Mittal as an “over-achiever” and believe professional stagnation may have influenced her move. Having moved rapidly from elite academic institutions and international finance to demanding district assignments, she may have found the slower phases of a bureaucratic career frustrating, they say.Her transfer from Mirzapur, extended wait for another posting, and eventual move from Deoria DM to special secretary in revenue department form part of that reading. But it’s just that: an interpretation offered by colleagues, not an explanation confirmed by Mittal.She has said her resignation was neither impulsive nor due to pressure.Her interests outside administration offer some clues, though not necessarily an answer. Mittal is the author of, “The Crafted Genius”, a book about preparation, discipline and resilience. Her social-media posts frequently discuss parenting, while her writing has examined what formal education fails to teach — emotional regulation, communication, financial management, loneliness and mental health.What comes next?Mittal has indicated that writing, teaching and social service could be among the avenues she explores next.Politics is another possibility being discussed, particularly in Mirzapur, where her resignation has revived memories of her tenure. Abhinav Tripathi, pradhan of Dhawespur Kakrahi, says he would like Mittal to contest an election from the district and would contribute to her campaign if she did.The proximity of the 2027 UP assembly polls has inevitably added to that speculation. Mittal, however, has said nothing to suggest that a political debut is imminent.Her farewell note offers only one certainty: she may have surrendered the office through which she pursued her idea of public service, but she does not see herself as having surrendered the idea itself.“The position may be gone,” she wrote, “but the dream this country’s soil gave me will not leave me.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: In 1973, former Army diver Eric Shaw began dropping donated boats off Gibraltar; over 30 vessels later, the sandy seabed had become a fish nursery
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how former Army diver Eric Shaw's initiative in 1973 transformed Gibraltar's sandy seabed into a thriving artificial reef, providing a habitat for diverse marine life and reshaping ecological dynamics in the region.
articles.body: In 1973, former Army diver Eric Shaw looked at Gibraltar’s largely sandy seabed and saw an opportunity to give marine life somewhere to settle, hide and breed. His solution was unusual: use unwanted boats to build an artificial reef. What began as an experiment eventually developed into a major underwater habitat, with more than 30 vessels intentionally sunk around Gibraltar. The project is now regarded as one of Europe’s earliest artificial reef programmes.From empty seabed to artificial reefShaw’s idea was based on a straightforward ecological challenge. A largely sandy seabed offers fewer hard surfaces, crevices and sheltered spaces than a rocky reef, limiting the range of habitats available to marine organisms. According to Shaw, quoted by The Guardian, the area had been mostly sand with little visible life, prompting him to create an “oasis” where marine species could breed and colonise. Old boats provided a practical way to introduce solid structures to the seabed, creating surfaces and shelter that could gradually be occupied by marine life.The first vessels were donated locally, allowing the reef to expand gradually over the following decades. Rather than treating 1973 as the start of the formal government programme, it is more accurate to describe it as the year Shaw began developing the idea. The Government of Gibraltar dates the construction of its Artificial Reef Project to 1975 and says that more than 30 vessels have since been intentionally sunk and strategically positioned to enhance marine biodiversity and provide shelter for marine life. Before a vessel is submerged, it is carefully prepared to minimise environmental risks, with potentially polluting or detachable materials, including fuels, lubricants and loose equipment, removed beforehand.The structures provide something the original seabed lacked: hard surfaces. Organisms can attach themselves to the hulls, while holes, shaded spaces and gaps offer shelter for smaller animals. As these organisms become established, they can provide food and habitat for other species, allowing a more complex marine community to develop. Research published in Estuarine and Coastal Marine Science similarly found that artificial structures can help organisms colonise otherwise barren areas by providing solid surfaces, shelter and food. The study examined artificial substrates rather than Gibraltar specifically, but its findings illustrate the ecological principle behind Shaw’s project.A new home for marine lifeOver the decades, the vessels became established as artificial reef structures that supported a growing range of marine life. HM Government of Gibraltar reports that the artificial reef programme, which began in the 1970s, was associated with a dramatic increase in mid-water and bottom-dwelling species, as well as a rise in sessile organisms living on the reef structures themselves. One assessment recorded 12 vertebrate and 22 invertebrate species in the area before the reef was established, compared with 54 vertebrate and 55 invertebrate species after it was in place.The ecological significance of the project lies in this gradual accumulation of life. A bare or relatively simple seabed is transformed as the artificial structures provide places for organisms to settle. Those organisms then become part of the food web, while the physical complexity of the reef provides shelter for juvenile and adult animals. Therefore, the project also demonstrates why artificial reefs are increasingly considered in marine habitat management. They can introduce structure into environments where natural hard habitat is limited. However, they are not automatically equivalent to natural reefs, and their success depends on location, materials, water movement and how the structures are managed.When conservation became controversialGibraltar reef ended up getting entangled in a bigger conflict altogether. In 2013, there was controversy regarding the setting of other concrete blocks in the waters off Gibraltar by Spain. The Spanish fishermen complained that this was hindering their ability to fish, and the argument between Gibraltar and Spain grew bigger. This particular conflict shows us the importance of artificial reefs. While they do provide habitats for aquatic organisms and attract more life in general, they also affect how the animals interact in the area. The fish that tend to form around these structures may end up changing the patterns of fishing in the region.However, the basic premise of Shaw’s reef-building idea was relatively simple. Instead of trying to engineer an entire ecosystem, he introduced solid structures that gave marine organisms surfaces on which to settle and spaces in which to shelter. Over time, the approach became part of Gibraltar’s broader efforts to enhance marine habitat and biodiversity. The project later became the centre of a diplomatic dispute in 2013, when the Gibraltar government placed dozens of concrete blocks on the seabed to create another artificial reef. Spanish fishermen protested, arguing that the blocks restricted access to fishing grounds they had traditionally used, while Gibraltar said the structures were intended to protect fish stocks and marine life. What began with Shaw’s attempt to provide structure on a largely barren seabed had therefore developed into a much larger conservation effort, while also becoming entangled in the long-running political tensions surrounding Gibraltar.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Cuba has opened its real estate sector to foreign investment as part of a sweeping package of economic reforms aimed at tackling a severe crisis and attracting private capital.The reforms, announced by the communist government in June, began taking effect this week through a series of decrees, resolutions and regulations. They come as Cuba struggles with shortages and an economic downturn following months of a US fuel blockade.Under the changes, foreign investors can now invest in Cuban real estate, marking a significant shift for an economy where the state has traditionally played a dominant role, reported AFP.The reforms also allow privately owned Cuban companies to work directly with foreign investors, hold accounts in overseas banks and import and export goods without going through government intermediaries.Previously, most foreign investors were required to form joint ventures with the Cuban state.The new measures further allow the creation of private companies employing more than 100 people and permit privately owned banks, pharmacies and gas stations.President Miguel Diaz-Canel has rejected suggestions that the reforms amount to a covert shift towards capitalism, saying they are intended to “preserve” socialism.The changes come as Cuba’s private sector has expanded to fill gaps left by the struggling state economy. More than 15,000 small and medium-sized enterprises currently operate on the island and employ more than a third of the working population, according to official data.Private companies now account for a major share of food and fuel distribution, while the government is increasingly turning to private and foreign investment to revive the wider economy.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 1995, Canada eradicated rats from British Columbia’s Langara Island; by 2004, ancient murrelet pairs had nearly doubled to 20,000–30,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Canada successfully eradicated rats from Langara Island, leading to a remarkable recovery of the ancient murrelet population. Learn about the innovative methods used for this conservation success.
articles.body: Islands have long been risky places for ground-nesting birds because, for most of evolutionary history, they had few predators to fear. That safety unravelled when humans began arriving by ship, because rats stowed away on vessels and found island seabird colonies easy prey. Few places show the damage more clearly than Langara Island, a remote island off the northern tip of Haida Gwaii in British Columbia, where one seabird population collapsed and later rebounded within a few decades.Rats reached Langara Island in the middle of the twentieth century, most likely as stowaways aboard fishing boats or log barges operating nearby. The island hosted one of the largest breeding colonies of ancient murrelets, small seabirds that dig burrows in forest soil and return to them under cover of darkness to avoid predators. Rats easily found the burrows and fed on eggs and chicks. Canada's own species assessment, published through the Government of Canada, attributes the roughly ninety per cent decline recorded in the Langara murrelet population directly to rat predation that built up over the following decades. Surveys conducted by conservation biologists in the 1980s found that large sections of Langara's own colony had already been abandoned, with searched burrows containing the bones of murrelets killed by rats, a clear warning sign of how close the population was to collapsing entirely.A poison bait campaign across the islandFunding for the project came from an unlikely source, the legal settlement following the Nestucca oil spill, which gave Environment Canada the resources to attempt something ambitious across the whole island rather than just a small test plot. Crews set up bait stations roughly every hundred metres in a grid covering the entirety of Langara Island, loading each one with wax blocks containing the anticoagulant brodifacoum. Rats kept taking bait for twenty-six days before crews switched to protective bagged bait stations to finish the job. The main eradication effort took place through 1995, and follow-up monitoring over the following years found no further sign of rats anywhere on the island, a result that surprised even some of the biologists who had pushed for the project.Murrelets bounce backThe recovery that followed was faster than most conservationists had dared to expect. A separate academic analysis using controlled before and after comparisons against islands without eradication programmes found the estimated population had jumped from roughly thirteen thousand birds in 1999 to around twenty-four thousand by 2004, a pace of growth of about thirteen per cent a year, according to figures compiled through the Conservation Evidence database, run by the University of Cambridge. Other burrow-nesting species that had vanished entirely from the island, including Cassin's auklet, also began reappearing in small numbers once the rats were gone. Langara has since become something of a template for island restoration efforts across Haida Gwaii and beyond, though Parks Canada has since had to deal with rats reinvading some of the smaller islands nearby, a reminder that keeping an island rat-free can be just as demanding as clearing it in the first place.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
